title: The viral '80% of German flak crews died' claim
claim: Roughly 80% of German anti-aircraft crew members died during the Second World War.
scope_note: This record reconstructs a visible online propagation chain. It does not establish the true aggregate mortality rate of German flak crews.

nodes.role: visible early node in current online propagation chain
early public challenge to the statistic and to imagery provenance
downstream article visibly using the YouTube material
condensed downstream summary of the viral video
later independent investigation reporting inability to trace the 80% figure to relevant German or scholarly records checked
documents nearby but different high flak-casualty percentages among Allied aircrew
archival orientation for United States Strategic Bombing Survey records
documents adolescent Flakhelfer and specific crew experience without establishing aggregate 80% mortality

current_findings: The 80% German flak-crew mortality claim circulates widely online.
At least one article and automated summary are downstream of the viral video and are not independent corroboration.
Contemporary viewers identified an imagery-provenance problem in the viral presentation.
A later independent researcher reported being unable to trace the 80% figure to German military, Luftwaffe personnel, or post-war academic records checked.
Authoritative sources support nearby facts about flak danger and Allied casualties but do not, in the sources checked for this record, establish the claimed aggregate German crew mortality rate.
unknowns: The true aggregate mortality rate of German anti-aircraft crews.
Whether an earlier source predating the identified online chain contains the 80% figure.
Whether the 80% figure arose by mutation from a different casualty statistic.
The completeness of surviving late-war German personnel and casualty records relevant to this question.
correction_rule: Bring stronger evidence. Update the record visibly without erasing the earlier claim, propagation chain, or correction history.
